title: 〜かったです・〜でした — "it was …"
explanation: To say something was a certain way, an い-adjective swaps its last い for かったです: たのしい → たのしかったです ("it was fun"), and くないです becomes くなかったです ("it wasn't"). いい is irregular: よかったです and よくなかったです. な-adjectives work like nouns, with でした and じゃなかったです (ひまでした). い-adjectives never take でした, so don't say おいしいでした. These are the polite forms; the casual versions (たのしかった, ひまだった) come with the plain past.

title: 〜へ — "toward"
explanation: へ (written with the kana he but said "e") marks the direction you are heading, with moving verbs like いく, くる and かえる. There it can swap with に: にほんへいきます and にほんにいきます mean the same thing, and へ just feels a little more like "toward". You'll also see it on signs and cards: にほんへようこそ ("welcome to Japan"), ゆいさんへ ("to Yui"). に still does the jobs へ can't, such as times (しちじに) and where things are. title: Casual speech — talking with your partner
explanation: With your partner, family and close friends, Japanese drops です and ます. Verbs use the dictionary form (たべます → たべる), い-adjectives just lose です (おいしい, never おいしいだ), and nouns and な-adjectives take だ or nothing at all (やすみだよ). Questions have no か and usually no だ: just let your voice rise at the end (いく？, げんき？), and は and を often drop out too (コーヒーのむ？). Add ね, よ, だよ or だね to sound warm, and keep です and ます for strangers, shop staff and the role-plays.

title: 〜のうえ・〜のなか — where things are
pattern: 〜の{上|うえ}に・〜の{中|なか}に・〜の{隣|となり}に
explanation: To say where something is, name the reference point first and join the position word with の: テーブルのうえ is "on the table" (literally "the table's top"). The common ones are うえ (on, above), した (under), なか (in), まえ (in front of), うしろ (behind), となり (next to), よこ (beside) and ちかく (near). Add に and あります or います: for something new, use が (テーブルのうえにかぎがあります), and for something you're already talking about, use は and put it first (かぎはテーブルのうえにあります). In polite and casual speech alike you can also just end with です or だ: かぎはテーブルのうえです.

title: 〜て — the て-form, "and then"
explanation: The て-form links actions in order, like "and then": おきて、シャワーをあびます ("I get up and take a shower"). The last verb sets the tense and the politeness for the whole sentence, so the て-form itself works in both polite and casual speech. る-verbs swap る for て (たべる → たべて), and う-verbs change by their last sound: う, つ, る → って; む, ぶ, ぬ → んで; く → いて; ぐ → いで; す → して. The odd ones are いく → いって, する → して and くる → きて. Many later patterns are built on it, such as てから ("after doing") and くて for joining adjectives.

title: 〜から〜まで — "from … to"
explanation: から means "from" and まで means "until" or "as far as", for both times and places: くじからごじまで ("from nine to five"), うちからえきまで ("from home to the station"). Each one also works alone: なんじまで？ ("until what time?"), あしたから ("from tomorrow"). This から marks a starting point; a different から meaning "because" comes later, and that one follows a whole sentence instead of a time or a place. Both are fine in polite and casual speech.

title: 〜が — the subject particle
explanation: が marks the subject when it is the new information, especially the answer to "who?" or "which?". pattern: {何曜日|なんようび}・〜{月|がつ}〜{日|にち}・いつ

title: 〜ています — "is doing"

title: 〜から — "because, so"
explanation: Put から after a reason to mean "because" or "so": つかれたから、ねる ("I'm tired, so I'm going to bed"). The reason comes first and the result second, the opposite order to English "because". The reason can be plain or polite (さむいから or さむいですから), but nouns and な-adjectives need だ or です before から (あめだから). Ask why with どうして or casual なんで, and you can answer with just the reason plus から: おもしろいから ("because it's funny"). This is not the から that means "from", which comes after a time or a place; a softer "because", ので, comes later.

title: 〜は〜が〜 — "X has long hair"
explanation: To describe a feature of someone or something, Japanese says "as for X, Y is …": つまはかみがながい (literally "as for my wife, hair is long", so "my wife has long hair"). は marks who or what you're describing, and が marks the part or feature. It's how you talk about places (このみせはパスタがおいしい), the body (あたまがいたい, where わたしは is usually left out) and abilities (わたしはにほんごがすこしわかります). The が here marks the feature, not the answer to "who?" as in the earlier が lesson, and the pattern works the same in polite and casual speech.

title: 〜とおもう — "I think that …"

title: 〜てはいけない — "must not"

explanation: て-form + はいけません states a rule, "you must not": ここでしゃしんをとってはいけません ("you mustn't take photos here"). title: 〜のがすき — liking doing things
pattern: 〜のが{好|す}き・〜のが{上手|じょうず}
explanation: To talk about liking or being good at an activity, turn the verb into a thing with の: dictionary form + の + が + すき, as in りょうりするのがすきです ("I like cooking"). The same pattern works with きらい, じょうず (good at), へた (bad at), とくい (my strong point) and にがて (my weak point). Use じょうず about other people and とくい about yourself, because calling yourself じょうず sounds like boasting. To name a hobby, use しゅみは〜ことです ("my hobby is …ing"). This の is not the "X's" の; it just turns an action into a thing, in polite or casual speech.

title: Describing nouns with sentences
explanation: In Japanese, a whole sentence can sit in front of a noun to describe it: きのうみたえいが ("the movie we saw yesterday"). The describing part always comes before the noun and ends in a plain form, even in polite speech: えきのちかくにあるみせ ("the shop near the station"). な-adjectives keep their な (りょうりがじょうずなひと), and the doer inside the describing part takes が, not は: つまがつくったケーキ ("the cake my wife made"). Keep it to one describing sentence per noun for now.

title: 〜けど・〜が — "but"
explanation: けど joins two sentences that pull against each other: たかいけど、おいしい ("it's expensive, but it's good"). が does the same job but sounds more polite and is common in writing: たかいですが、おいしいです. Nouns and な-adjectives need だ or です first: あめだけど. At the very end of a sentence, けど softens it and leaves something unsaid, which is how Japanese politely hints "no": ちょっとたかいですけど… . To start a new sentence with "but", use でも instead; a stronger "even though" (のに) comes later.

title: 〜てから — "after doing"
explanation: て-form + から means "after doing" or "once I've done": ごはんをたべてから、でかけます ("I'll go out after I eat"). The plain て-form just lists actions in order; てから stresses that the first one is finished before the second starts. As with the plain て-form, the last verb sets the tense and the politeness. With a starting point in time it can also mean "since": にほんごをはじめてから ("since I started Japanese"). Don't confuse it with から "because", which follows a plain or polite form (たべたから), not a て-form.

title: もう・まだ — "already", "not yet"

title: 〜という — "say", "called"
explanation: いう means "say", and what was said goes before と. To report what someone said, put a plain form before と: つまはつかれたといいました ("my wife said she was tired"); for someone's exact words, put them in 「」 brackets. いっていました ("was saying") is the everyday way to pass on a message: ともだちはこないといっていました. いう also names things: noun + という + noun means "a … called …" (さくらというみせ), and 〜はにほんごでなんといいますか asks "how do you say … in Japanese?". This is a different job from で for places and tools. title: 〜ている — states: married, living, knowing
pattern: {結婚|けっこん}している・{住|す}んでいる・{知|し}っている
explanation: Some verbs describe a change that happens in a moment, like getting married, moving somewhere or getting to know something. With these, ている describes the state left afterwards, not an action in progress: けっこんしています means "I'm married", not "I'm getting married". Learn the common ones as set phrases: すんでいます (live), しっています (know), もっています (have), つかれています (be tired), and for clothes きています, はいています and かけています (be wearing). Watch the odd one out: "I don't know" is しりません (casual しらない), not しっていません. In casual speech they shrink the same way as before: しってる？ すんでる.

title: 〜がほしい — "I want (a thing)"
explanation: ほしい means "want" for things: noun + が + ほしい (polite: ほしいです), as in あたらしいスマホがほしいです ("I want a new smartphone"). It's an い-adjective, so it changes like one: ほしかった (wanted), ほしくない (don't want). Use it about yourself, or to ask your partner (たんじょうび、なにがほしい？), but not to state what someone else wants: Japanese avoids speaking directly about other people's feelings. For wanting to do something, use 〜たい instead; wanting someone else to do something (〜てほしい) comes later.
